title: equals, hashCode, and compareTo
summary: Make your objects compare by value, work as HashMap and HashSet keys, and sort naturally.
intro: Two `new Point(1, 2)` objects are not equal until you say so. Three methods decide how your classes behave in comparisons and collections: `equals` for value equality and `hashCode` for `HashSet` and `HashMap`, both inherited from `Object`, and `compareTo` from the `Comparable` interface for sorting and `TreeSet`.

steps.title: Overriding equals

example.title: Raw points and real points
example.prompt: Read pairs of points and print `==`, the inherited `equals` of `RawPoint`, and the overridden `equals` of `Point` for each pair.
example.output:
(1, 2) vs (1, 2): == false, RawPoint equals false, Point equals true
(3, 4) vs (3, 5): == false, RawPoint equals false, Point equals false
(0, 0) vs (0, 0): == false, RawPoint equals false, Point equals true
example.explanation: Each pair builds two separate objects, so `==` is always `false`. `RawPoint` keeps the inherited `equals`, which is the same identity check, so it is `false` too even when the coordinates match. `Point` overrides `equals(Object)`: after the `instanceof` check and the cast it compares `x` and `y`, so (1, 2) equals (1, 2) and (3, 4) does not equal (3, 5).

practice.title: Matching cards
practice.prompt:
Give `Card` value equality and compare each pair of cards you read.

1. In `Card`, override `equals(Object o)` with `@Override`: return `true` when `this == o`, `false` when `o` is not a `Card`, and otherwise cast and compare both fields.
2. Both fields are `String`s, so compare them with `Objects.equals`, which also handles `null`. Ranks are case-sensitive, so `J` and `j` differ.
3. In `main`, for each pair print `a + " vs " + b`, then `: == ` and the result of `a == b`, then `, equals ` and the result of `a.equals(b)`.

Input:

```text
3
A hearts A hearts
10 spades 10 clubs
K diamonds Q diamonds
```

Expected output:

```text
A of hearts vs A of hearts: == false, equals true
10 of spades vs 10 of clubs: == false, equals false
K of diamonds vs Q of diamonds: == false, equals false
```

tests.stdin:
3
A hearts A hearts
10 spades 10 clubs
K diamonds Q diamonds
tests.output:
A of hearts vs A of hearts: == false, equals true
10 of spades vs 10 of clubs: == false, equals false
K of diamonds vs Q of diamonds: == false, equals false

tests.stdin:
2
Q clubs Q clubs
7 hearts 7 spades
tests.output:
Q of clubs vs Q of clubs: == false, equals true
7 of hearts vs 7 of spades: == false, equals false
J of spades vs j of spades: == false, equals false

hints: Copy the shape of `Point.equals` from the example and change `Point` to `Card`.
Compare each field with `Objects.equals(field, other.field)` and join the two checks with `&&`.
Wrap `a == b` in parentheses inside the concatenation so it is compared before it is joined.

steps.title: hashCode for maps and sets

example.title: Two kinds of point sets
example.prompt: Read points into a set of a class with only `equals` and a set of a class with `equals` and `hashCode`, then compare sizes, lookups, and a map count.
example.output:
equals only: size 5, contains (1, 2) false
equals and hashCode: size 3, contains (1, 2) true
Count of (1, 2): 2
example.explanation: `EqualsOnlyPoint` has a correct `equals` but the inherited identity `hashCode`, so every object hashes differently. The set never compares the two (1, 2) points and keeps all five, and a fresh `EqualsOnlyPoint(1, 2)` is not found. `Point` hashes with `Objects.hash(x, y)`, so equal points meet in the same bucket, `equals` spots the repeats, and only 3 distinct points remain. The same `hashCode` lets the `HashMap` find the key (1, 2) again with a brand new object, so `merge` counted it twice.

practice.title: Robot walk
practice.prompt:
Walk a robot on a grid from (0, 0) and report which cells it visited.

1. In `Cell`, override `equals(Object o)` to compare `x` and `y`, and override `hashCode` with `Objects.hash(x, y)`.
2. In `main`, record every cell the robot stands on, including the start, in a `Set<Cell>` built as a `HashSet`, and count visits per cell in a `Map<Cell, Integer>` built as a `HashMap`.
3. Print `Distinct cells: ` and the size of the set.
4. Print `Start visits: ` and the count for `new Cell(0, 0)`.
5. Print `Visited (1, 1): ` and whether the set contains `new Cell(1, 1)`.

Input:

```text
6
R U L D R R
```

Expected output:

```text
Distinct cells: 5
Start visits: 2
Visited (1, 1): true
```

tests.stdin:
6
R U L D R R
tests.output:
Distinct cells: 5
Start visits: 2
Visited (1, 1): true

Distinct cells: 2
Start visits: 3
Visited (1, 1): false

Distinct cells: 4
Start visits: 1
Visited (1, 1): false

hints: Without `hashCode`, every visit counts as a new cell and the totals come out too high.
Add the start cell before the loop and the new cell after each move, and count with `merge` the same way the example does.
Look up with fresh objects such as `new Cell(0, 0)`: that works only because `equals` and `hashCode` compare values.

steps.title: Comparable and natural order

example.title: Sorting versions
example.prompt: Read version numbers like 1.10, sort them by major then minor, drop an exact duplicate with a `TreeSet`, and list them newest first.
example.explanation: `split("\\.")` splits on a literal dot, and the parts become numbers, so 1.10 sorts after 1.2. As plain strings it would sort first. `Collections.sort` uses `compareTo`: major first, then minor. The `TreeSet` sorts with the same `compareTo` and drops the second 1.2 because comparing it to the first returns 0. `Version` also overrides `equals` and `hashCode` on the same two fields, so `compareTo` returns 0 exactly when `equals` is true. `Collections.reverseOrder()` is a `Comparator` that flips the natural order.

practice.title: Race podium
practice.prompt:
Rank race results where some lines were entered twice by mistake.

1. In `Runner`, implement `compareTo`: lower `time` first, and on equal times order by `name` with `String`'s `compareTo`. The starter already overrides `equals` and `hashCode` on both fields.
2. In `main`, copy `runners` into a `Set<Runner>` built as a `TreeSet` to drop exact duplicates, then print `Runners: ` and its size.
3. Print the podium: the first three runners of the set (fewer if there are fewer), one per line as the place, `. `, and the runner, like `1. Ben 50`.
4. Copy the set into a new list, sort it with `Comparator.comparing(Runner::getName)`, and print `By name: ` followed by the list. After duplicates are dropped, names are unique.

Input:

```text
6
Ana 52
Ben 50
Cy 50
Ana 52
Dee 61
Eve 55
```

Expected output:

```text
Runners: 5
1. Ben 50
2. Cy 50
3. Ana 52
By name: [Ana 52, Ben 50, Cy 50, Dee 61, Eve 55]
```

tests.stdin:

Ana 52
Ben 50
Cy 50
Ana 52
Dee 61
Eve 55
tests.output:

1. Ben 50
2. Cy 50
3. Ana 52
By name: [Ana 52, Ben 50, Cy 50, Dee 61, Eve 55]

Runners: 2

hints: Follow `Version.compareTo`: `Integer.compare` on `time`, and only when that is 0 return `name.compareTo(other.name)`.
Without the name tie-breaker, Ben and Cy both finish in 50, compare as 0, and the `TreeSet` keeps only one of them.
Loop over the set with a `place` counter and `break` once it passes 3.

recap:
- The inherited `equals` is the same as `==`: true only for the same object.
- Override `public boolean equals(Object o)` with `@Override`. An `equals(Point p)` parameter is an overload that collections never call.
- Shape: `this == o` shortcut, `instanceof` check, cast, then compare fields.
- Use `Objects.equals(a, b)` for reference fields that may be `null`.
- Override `hashCode` with `Objects.hash(...)` on the same fields. Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
- Without `hashCode`, a `HashSet` keeps equal duplicates and a `HashMap` cannot find equal keys.
- Print a `HashSet` or `HashMap` only through order-free results such as `size()`, `contains(...)`, and `get(...)`.
- `implements Comparable<X>` with `compareTo` built from `Integer.compare` and tie-breakers gives a natural order.
- `Collections.sort`, `Collections.max`, `TreeSet`, and `TreeMap` use `compareTo`, and the tree collections treat a `compareTo` of 0 as a duplicate. Keep `compareTo` consistent with `equals`.
- Pass a `Comparator` such as `Collections.reverseOrder()` or `Comparator.comparing(...)` for any other order.
